question: What regulatory or legal problems do robotic construction processes run into?

answer.answer:
Regulatory and legal exposure (RI18, a Risk) is not something robots run into after the fact: in every cited path it sits upstream, as a compliance condition that has to be satisfied before the work can proceed. Four things are conditioned on it: collaborative working alongside people (CO6), bespoke robot technology built for the job (AT3), additive manufacturing (PR3) and on-site fabrication (PR8), all on standards evidence, and all four are gating rather than enabling. The retrieval terms themselves, a robotic arm (RE2), robotic assembly (PR4), robotic drilling (PR19) and an unmanned mobile vehicle (RE15), carry no cited regulatory edge of their own; robotic assembly's only cited organisational requirement is the delivery model and work culture (RI12), carried by just 2 of the 50 cases. In the deployed Japanese record the relation runs the other way round: regulation is repeatedly recorded as the reason a process was adopted, including a timber joinery and assembly line at technology readiness level 9 and a concrete 3D printing process at level 7.

**What the regulatory exposure attaches to.** 12 of the 50 coded cases draw on RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (Risk) [1], and of the 8 dependency edges in the graph graded 'standard', which are listed in full, 4 gate and 4 enable or mitigate [1]. All four gating edges run into RI18, so on standards evidence the regulatory requirement is the single most common precondition in that grade:

- AT3 "Bespoke DFAB technology" (Attribute) dependsOn RI18, carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases: robot technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance [1]. This is the broadest exposure by carried cases: building your own robot pulls you into the industrial robot safety regime before anything is installed.
- CO6 "Human-robot interaction" (Condition) dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50: human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [1]. The asymmetry here is worth stating: 32 of the 50 cases draw on CO6 [1] and 12 on RI18, but only 2 carry the edge joining them, so the collaborative-safety compliance link is asserted in the literature and exhibited by very few of the coded cases.
- PR3 "Additive manufacturing" (Process) dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50: 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability [1].
- PR8 "On-site DFAB" (Process) dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50: on-site 3D concrete printing deployment proceeds via an alternative-means approval pathway in the building code [1].

RI18 carries 5 cited dependency edges in total [1], so one further edge exists that was not gathered here; the four above are complete for the standards grade only.

**Safety obligations, which the same standards discharge.** RI20 "Work safety concern" (Risk) carries 3 inbound and 0 outbound edges, all listed, and 13 of the 50 cases draw on it [1]. All three are mitigations: CO6 mitigates RI20, carried by 4 of the 50, through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits [1]; CO2 "3D scanning/RFID/sensing" mitigates RI20, carried by 7 of the 50, through speed-and-separation monitoring that maintains a minimum protective distance [1]; AT10 "Human assistance" mitigates RI20, carried by 8 of the 50, via a passive exoskeleton that reduced lumbar erector spinae activity and is proposed as an ergonomic intervention [1]. So the same collaborative-robot standard that creates the compliance burden also supplies the two engineering routes out of the contact-injury risk.

**What the retrieval terms do and do not carry.** Retrieval widened "robotic construction processes" to the robotic arm, robotic assembly, robotic drilling and the unmanned mobile vehicle, and this changes what can be claimed: none of them has a cited edge to RI18. PR4 "Robotic assembly" carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound edges, all listed, and 13 of the 50 draw on it [1]; its only requirement of an institutional kind is RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", carried by 2 of the 50, on the finding that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1], while 16 of the 50 cases draw on RI12 in its own right [1]. RE2 "Robotic arm" carries 1 inbound and 1 outbound edge, both listed, and 22 of the 50 draw on it [1]; 9 of the 50 draw on PR19 "Robotic drilling", which carries no dependency edges [1], and 25 of the 50 draw on RE15 "Unmanned mobile vehicle", which also carries none [1]. The cited dependency layer is sparse, 100 edges touching 68 of the 140 enablers, which is a property of the literature and not of the record [1], so the absence of a regulatory edge on drilling or on a mobile vehicle is an unwritten connection, not an absence of exposure.

**The deployed record.** Regulation appears in the census profiles as the challenge a deployment was adopted to address, not as an obstacle it hit. Among the steel-frame processes, census_RXH5-1 was adopted to address regulation, performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core, and is at technology readiness level 9 [2], with Firm_027 as its manufacturer and steel as its material [3]; census_RXM33-2 was adopted to address regulation and performs assembly, material handling, steelwork and welding on the structural core at technology readiness level 7 [4], developed by Firm_066 [3]. In timber, census_RXT4-1 was adopted to address integration, market and regulation, performs assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting on the structural core, and is at technology readiness level 9 [5], developed by Firm_174 [3]. The clearest match to the additive-manufacturing certification path is census_RXM4-3, adopted to address regulation, performing 3D printing, assembly and concrete work on the structural core at technology readiness level 7 [6], manufactured by Firm_115 and recorded as the census record of RP15 [3], which is deployed as a mobile robot and off-site at technology readiness level 7 [7]. Off-site steel assembly appears as RP10, adopted to address integration and regulation, performing assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core off-site at technology readiness level 9 [8], and RP5, adopted to address cost, integration and regulation, working on the structural core off-site at technology readiness level 9 [9], recorded as census_RXH9-1b under Firm_160 [3].

A limit to note: these deployed records give the challenge addressed, the materials, the firm and the readiness level, but the context does not link any of them to particular enablers, so how many of them draw on RI18, CO6 or PR3 is not in front of me.

**Deployed evidence.** Selected by filtering the coded records, not by similarity. 15 records in the graph carry Regulation as their adoption driver; all are listed below.
- RP10, adopted to address integration, regulation; performs assembly, steelwork, welding; works on the structural core; deployed off-site; at technology readiness level 9.
